summary: This informational memo defines the common architecture for Multicast Security key management. It introduces the group security association, a shared set of security settings for a group, and describes the protocols that establish it. The architecture supports security protocols at various layers.

eli5.summary: When many people share a secret message, they all need the same key. This document describes how a group can get and manage that shared key.

questions: what is a group security association
how does multicast group rekeying work
what is the difference between registration sa and rekey sa
subtitle: The common blueprint for how a group of receivers gets, and keeps getting, the shared keys that protect multicast traffic.

tldr.problem: Secure group and multicast applications need every legitimate member to hold up-to-date keys, while members join and leave and the group may be very large. One-to-one key exchange protocols do not cover this.
tldr.mechanism: A Group Controller and Key Server (GCKS) authenticates joining members in a unicast registration protocol and hands them a group security association (GSA). An optional rekey protocol later pushes updated keys to the whole group.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an informational architecture, not a protocol. Concrete protocols are meant to be specialized from it, and the RFC itself warns that novelty and complexity are the biggest risks.

today: RFC 4046 is an Informational architecture document, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It specifies no wire protocol itself, so concrete group key management protocols such as GDOI (RFC 3547) are the instantiations it points to.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This document defines a common architecture for Multicast Security (MSEC) key management protocols that support application-, transport- and network-layer security protocols. It also defines the group security association (GSA) and describes the protocols that establish one. The framework lets group key management protocols be designed modularly for different settings, and it can serve one-to-many, many-to-many or one-to-one communication.

It is based on the group controller or key server model of GKMP (RFC 2094) and assumed by key management algorithms such as LKH (RFC 2627), OFT and MARKS. Other approaches, such as the highly distributed Cliques protocol and broadcast key management, are not considered.

Different security protocols benefit from different group key management systems, for example SRTP (RFC 3711) and IPsec. Some run key management over a pre-established secure channel such as TLS or IPsec, some over SIP or RTSP, and some want a lightweight protocol with few round trips.
sections.eli5: Many different programs need to share secret keys with a whole group. This paper gives one common plan that all of them can follow.

sections.title: What a Group Key Protocol Must Do
sections.content:
A group key management protocol should give legitimate members the up-to-date cryptographic state they need for secrecy and authentication. The RFC lists 12 requirements that are neither exhaustive nor applicable to all applications. Among them:

  • Members receive security associations containing keys, policy and an index.
  • Keys have a pre-determined lifetime and may be refreshed.
  • Key material is delivered secretly, with integrity, and from a verifiably authorized source.
  • The protocol resists replay and denial-of-service attacks.
  • Joining and leaving are supported: removed members should lose access to the key material, and added members may optionally be denied the key material used before they joined.
  • Group rekeying should scale without unicast exchanges between every member and the GCKS.
  • It resists collusion among excluded members and non-members, and offers a way to recover from compromise.

Two non-requirements are named: technical protection measures (TPM), such as copy protection that keeps keys from the device user, and broadcast key management with no back channel. The architecture assumes IP operation with two-way communication, and covers large single-sender groups such as source-specific multicast groups.
sections.eli5: The club's password system has to keep the password secret, change it when people come and go, and keep working even when the club is huge.

sections.title: The Overall Design
sections.content:
The design uses a group controller model with a single group owner as root of trust. The owner designates a Group Controller and Key Server (GCKS) for member registration and rekeying. The goal is to give members an up-to-date Data SA, which secures the group traffic. Two protocols do the work:

  • The registration protocol is a unicast exchange in which the GCKS and a joining member mutually authenticate. If the member is authorized, the GCKS supplies what is needed to initialize the Data SA and/or a Rekey SA.
  • The rekey protocol lets the GCKS update the Data SA or Rekey SA, by multicast or unicast, after membership changes, policy changes, new keys or key expiration.

There are three SAs. The Registration SA is a unicast SA between the GCKS and each member that protects registration. The Rekey SA protects rekey messages and is the only optional one. The Data SA protects the traffic. Together the three compose the GSA.

Two key types matter. The key encryption key (KEK) protects rekey messages, and traffic protection keys (TPKs) protect the data. The GCKS may be co-located with a member or separate, and may delegate to subordinate GCKSs. Scalability comes from decoupling registration from rekeying, optional multicast key distribution, and spreading the GCKS role over several entities.
sections.eli5: The club leader checks your name at the door (registration), gives you the secret password, and later whispers new passwords to everyone at once (rekey).

sections.title: Registration and Rekey in Practice
sections.content:
A registration protocol can be built on any secure-channel protocol such as IPsec or TLS. GDOI (RFC 3547) reuses IKE Phase 1 as the secure channel, while MIKEY and GSAKMP use authenticated Diffie-Hellman exchanges tailored for key download. Some registration protocols tunnel through SIP or RTSP to save setup time, and SIP requires a tunneled protocol to use at most one roundtrip (two messages). There are trade-offs: perfect forward secrecy and identity protection cost performance, while one- or two-message setups have low latency but may need more infrastructure or give less security. Replay protection uses a timestamp (needing synchronized clocks) or a sequence number (needing state); challenge-response with nonces avoids synchronized clocks when three or more messages are used.

For rekeying, messages are encrypted with the group KEK and authenticated with a MAC from the group authentication key or with a digital signature, with a sequence number covering replay. Reliable delivery options include repeating the message, a reliable multicast protocol, or FEC. A member that notices a gap can re-register, open a simple unprotected connection to the GCKS, or fetch the messages from a public site. The RFC also discusses implosion, where many members contact the GCKS at once, and suggests random waits or local repair servers.

Key management algorithms (GKMAs) make rekeying scalable. Stateful ones such as LKH and OFT depend on past updates, stateless ones such as Subset Difference do not, and self-healing ones let a member rebuild a lost message from earlier and later ones.
sections.eli5: If you miss the whisper with the new password, you can walk back to the leader and ask, or read it from a notice board. When the whole club asks at once, they should wait a random moment so the leader is not swamped.

sections.title: What a Group Security Association Contains
sections.content:
The architecture defines the interfaces between registration, rekey and data security protocols in terms of their SAs. Without a Rekey SA, the registration protocol initializes and updates the Data SAs. With one, registration initializes Rekey SAs and zero or more Data SAs, and the rekey protocol updates the Rekey SA and establishes the rest.

The Rekey SA holds policy (the group key management algorithm, KEK encryption algorithm and key length, authentication algorithm, control group address, rekey server address), the group identity, one or more KEKs with key IDs and lifetimes, an authentication key, replay protection state with sequence numbers, and an SPI. The pair of group identity and SPI uniquely identifies a Rekey SA, and the SPI changes each time the KEKs change.

The Data SA carries the group and source identity, the TPKs or information to derive them, data authentication keys, sequence numbers and an SPI where the data protocol uses one, and policy such as encryption and authentication algorithms. Examples of data security protocols are IPsec ESP and SRTP.

Group policy itself lives outside the protocol, in a policy repository, and is described by the Group Security Policy Token document.
sections.eli5: The group's bundle is like a locker with the current password, the date it expires, and a label saying which version it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limits
sections.content:
This memo describes an architecture that will be instantiated in one or more protocols, which must be protected against man-in-the-middle, connection hijacking, replay, reflection and denial-of-service attacks. It does not address implementation attacks such as buffer overflows.

Group settings add new problems: a member may disclose group secrets, and one member may impersonate a sender or the GCKS. GCKS messages should not be authenticated with shared symmetric secrets unless all members can be trusted not to impersonate the GCKS or each other. The architecture assumes no negotiation of cryptographic parameters, so group owners set policy externally, and members must decide what minimum security they accept before joining.

The registration protocol should be as secure as base protocols like IKE, IPsec, TLS or SSL. The rekey protocol is new and has unknown risks. The RFC concludes that novelty and complexity are the biggest risks to group key management protocols.
sections.eli5: A shared password is only as safe as the weakest member, and anyone in the club who knows it could pretend to be the leader. That is why the paper asks for careful design.

items.title: Registration SA
items.text: Unicast SA between the GCKS and a member; protects the registration protocol.

items.text: Protects rekey messages; holds KEKs, an authentication key and replay protection state.

items.text: Holds the traffic protection keys and policy for the data security protocol.
